# Iterative Coding


## Load libraries
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
```

## for loops
```{r}
for (index in sequence) {  # for is the function, i is the index (changes with each iteration)
  command to repeat
}
```

### simple example for loop
```{r}
print(paste("The year is", 2000))
```
#### Put it in a loop, create sequence (vector) "years"
```{r}
years <- c(2015:2021)

for (i in years) {
  print(paste("The year is", i))
}
```
#### Create a dataframe - pre-allocate space to fill one row at a time. This is flexible, you never want to hard-code.
```{r}
year_data <- tibble(year = rep(NA, length(years)), #rep = repeats
                    year_name = rep(NA, length(years)))

year_data
```

#### Make it broader - use sequence along this particular df
```{r}
for (i in seq_along(years)) { # seq_along, move along the sequence 1-2-3-4 (if you have 0 in your data you'll get secret error)
  year_data$year_name[i] <- paste("The year is", years[i])
}

year_data
```

#### Fill in the column too
```{r}
for (i in seq_along(years)) {
  year_data$year_name[i] <- paste("The year is", years[i])
  year_data$year[i] <- years[i]
}

year_data
```

### Use loops to read in multiple csv files
```{r}
testdata <- read_csv(here("Week_13", "Data", "cond_data", "011521_CT316_1pcal.csv"))

glimpse(testdata)
```
### List files in a directory
```{r}
# Point to the folder on the computer
CondPath <- here("Week_13", "Data", "cond_data")

# List all files in that path matching a pattern (here, anything with .csv)
# You can use regex to be more specific about filenames # can use any regex to only find files with certain words/letters/numbers
files <- dir(path = CondPath, pattern = ".csv")

files
```

### Pre-allocate space for the loop
```{r}
# One row for each file and 3 columns
cond_data <- tibble(filename = rep(NA, length(files)),
                    mean_temp = rep(NA, length(files)),
                    mean_sal = rep(NA, length(files)))

cond_data
```

### Write the basic code first
```{r}
# Test by reading in the first file (this is baseR)
raw_data <- read_csv(paste0(CondPath, "/", files[1])) #paste 0 leaves NO space 
head(raw_data)
```
```{r}
mean_temp <- mean(raw_data$Temperature, na.rm = TRUE) #baseR
mean_temp
```

### Turn it into a for loop
```{r}
for (i in seq_along(files)) { # loop over each file (1, 2, 3)


}
```

```{r}
for (i in seq_along(files)) {

  raw_data <- read_csv(paste0(CondPath, "/", files[i]))
  glimpse(raw_data) # glimpse in a for loop SLOWS down the loops, hashtag after checking

}
```

```{r}
for (i in seq_along(files)) {

  raw_data <- read_csv(paste0(CondPath, "/", files[i]))

  cond_data$filename[i] <- files[i] # add filenames for each row
  cond_data$mean_temp[i] <- mean(raw_data$Temperature, na.rm = TRUE) # add means
  cond_data$mean_sal[i] <- mean(raw_data$Salinity, na.rm = TRUE)

}

cond_data
```

## Purrr
Now we will do the exact same thing, but with tidyverse style language. map() as in layer things on top of each other. 

### map functions
The pattern of looping over a vector, doing something to each element and saving the results is so common that purrr provides a family of functions to do it for you. There is one function for each type of output:


Map some function onto each row in a dataframe. 

### simple ex
```{r}
set.seed(3817) # makes the random numbers reproducible
1:10 |> # the vector to iterate over, 10 sets of random numbers 
  map(rnorm, n = 15) # 15 random numbers from a normal distribution, in a list
```
1. calc the mean of each list element
```{r}
set.seed(3817) # makes the random numbers reproducible
1:10 |> # the vector to iterate over
  map(rnorm, n = 15) |> 
  map_dbl(mean) # result is now a vector of type "double"
```
2. same way, just make your own function
```{r}
set.seed(3817)
1:10 |>
  map(function(x) rnorm(15, x)) |> # make your own function
  map_dbl(mean)
```
3. use a formula when you want to change the arg within the function
```{r}
set.seed(3817)
1:10 |>
  map(~ rnorm(15, .x)) |> # changes the arguments inside the function
  map_dbl(mean)
```

### Bring in files using purrr instead of a for loop
Find the files: Already have CondPath and filed in values from earlier code chunk.
```{r}
CondPath <- here("Week_13", "data", "cond_data")
files <- dir(path = CondPath, pattern = ".csv")

files
```

Or get the full file names in one less step (purrr wants full path:
```{r}
files <- dir(path = CondPath, pattern = ".csv", full.names = TRUE) # saves the entire path
files
```

### Read in the files
```{r}
data <- files |>
  set_names() |> # names each list element with its file name
  map(read_csv) |> # a list of 3 dataframes
  list_rbind(names_to = "filename") # stack them; list names go in a "filename" column - first column name 

data
```
### Calc means
```{r}
data <- files |>
  set_names() |>
  map(read_csv) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "filename") |>
  group_by(filename) |>
  summarise(mean_temp = mean(Temperature, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_sal = mean(Salinity, na.rm = TRUE))

data
```

### Shortcut: readr
EVERY FILE HAS TO HAVE THE EXACT SAME COLUMNS 
```{r}
data <- read_csv(files, id = "filename") |>
  group_by(filename) |>
  summarise(mean_temp = mean(Temperature, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_sal = mean(Salinity, na.rm = TRUE))
data
```

### Other uses: a plot for every file (purrr)
Maps and loops are awesome for more complicated processes too. For example, you can make a plot from each file and save it automatically.

When you want a function’s side effect (saving a file, printing) rather than a returned value, use walk() instead of map().
```{r}
file_names <- dir(path = CondPath, pattern = ".csv") # just the file names

save_temp_plot <- function(file_name) {
  site_name <- str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv")

  p <- read_csv(paste0(CondPath, "/", file_name)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = Temperature)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(title = site_name, x = "Date", y = "Temperature (°C)")

  ggsave(here("Week_13", "Outputs", paste0(site_name, "_temp.png")),
         plot = p, width = 6, height = 4)
}

walk(file_names, save_temp_plot)
```
run `save_temp_plot(file_names[1])` first, once it works for one file, then add `walk()` . Walk is faster than for loop

### Other uses: a plot for every file (for loop)
```{r}
file_names <- dir(path = CondPath, pattern = ".csv") # just the file names

for (i in seq_along(file_names)) {

  raw_data <- read_csv(paste0(CondPath, "/", file_names[i]))

  site_name <- str_remove(file_names[i], "\\.csv") # drop ".csv" for the title

  p <- ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = date, y = Temperature)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(title = site_name, x = "Date", y = "Temperature (°C)")

  ggsave(here("Week_13", "Outputs", paste0(site_name, "_temp.png")),
         plot = p, width = 6, height = 4)
}
```
check 
```{r}
dir(here("Week_13", "Outputs"), pattern = "_temp.png")
```
